content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper applies the 3D autoencoder model from Lai et al. into a robotics setting. The model is pretrained on novel view synthesis on multiview data. It's then finetuned on simulated data and sim2real performance is measured. The model outperforms selected baselines pretrained on 2D tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The authors perform experiments on various datasets including MetaWorld and xArm, as well as a sim2real setting. This means that significant amount work was put into this paper.

Weakness:
- Regarding xArm experiment: why in life experiment, MOCO feature's performance consistently getting worse after the half way point?
- Figure 5's curves seem to suggest that in push, peg in box, reach, the performances are quite similar. I wonder why the number seems so different for these tasks in table 1 left. 
- Overall, I think the selected baselines are a bit limited, and it's not a good choice to have only 2D trained features. Cited prior works like "3d neural scene representations for visuomotor control" seem to be great candidate to perform well in the given simulation task as well as sim2real setting. Many other prior works lie Tung et al, as well as uncited works like "Learning 3D Dynamic Scene Representations for Robot Manipulation" can also serve as competitive baselines.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is quite clear, quality is good and reproducibility seems high.
However, I don't think the works is very novel. The key component is from Deep Video Autoencoder.
content.summary_of_the_review: The main comparison made are again 2D only encoder, which ignores a plethora of works in 3D scene representations for robot learning.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The proposed paper introduces a novel approach for employing a learned 3D representation for robotic motor control. The introduced self-supervised approach consists of a pretraining phase to learn a 3D voxel representation and a fine-tuning phase that optimizes the 3D representation as part of RL policy training. The approach is mainly tested on a manipulation tasks in simulation. Additionally, a zero-shot transfer to a real robot setup is explored. The method is validated on Meta-World tasks and on four robotic manipulation tasks in simulation and in real.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The topic this paper addresses, namely, the representation learning for robotic control, is important and interesting. 
- The idea of pretraining an object-centric 3D representation to then jointly fine-tune it with the RL policy training seems novel. 
- The paper discusses a thorough set of experiments and ablations studies that show the benefits of the proposed 3D representation. 
- Real robot experiments through sim2real transfer. 

Weaknesses: 

- The approach of using learned visual representations is not entirely novel and has been explored in other contexts. 
- The technical sections of the paper appear somewhat unpolished and more details should be provided. 
- The paper does not discuss any limitations of the proposed method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- In Figure 1 it is not clear from the caption what is meant by 'Real (Perturb)', not explanation is provided. 
- Section 4.1 (Architecture): What is 'C'?
- Section 4.1 (Architecture): What is meant by 'Now let I_tgt denote a target view of the same scene as I_src'?
- Section 4.1 (Architecture): In Eq. (3) what is \hat{I}?
- Section 4.1 (Training): What is meant by 'for most videos in the real world we can assume the structure does not change drastically'? Is this supposed to mean that the captured content does not change?
- Section 4.1 (Training): It is not clear what is meant by 'we constrain the interval between any two sampled views by a bound b, such that the number of skipped frames are randomized but bounded'. What is the randomization strategy used here? Please provide more details. 
- The setup of the discussed experiments seems sound and the results are interesting and plausible. I also appreciate the discussion toward robustness of the proposed approach. However, I am missing an in-depth discussion of the limitations of the method.  
- The paper should also discuss the following paper as it uses a similar approach as the one proposed: X. Yan, M. Khansari, J. Hsu, Y. Gong, Y. Bai, S. Pirk, H. Lee, Data-Efficient Learning for Sim-to-Real Robotic Grasping using Deep Point Cloud Prediction Networks, 2019

As is not enough information is provided to allow for reproducing the proposed method.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this is an interesting paper that can be accepted to ICLR 2023. The text is well-written, the experiments are sound, and the results are promising. However, there are a few shortcomings that I would like to see address prior to acceptance: 1) Section 4.1. would benefit from a careful pass of polishing the text. As detailed below, some symbols are not properly introduced, the grammar is off for some sentences and the paragraph could more carefully be written overall. Moreover, the current version of the paper does not discuss any limitations. To stimulate future work in the direction of the proposed method it would be beneficial to carefully discuss situations the current approach cannot handle well or at all.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to pre-train and finetune 3D representations for reinforcement learning of motor control tasks. In the pre-training phase, a 3D representation is learned on the CO3D dataset by reconstructing a target view from an input view. The 3D representation is then finetuned for motor-control tasks via joint RL + 3D representation learning objectives. Experiments are performed in simulation on Meta-World and xArm benchmarks. Sim2real results are demonstrated by transferring xArm policies to a real-robot.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths

* The idea is well motivated. 3D representations are crucial for robotic manipulation tasks and the proposed method offers a self-supervised way to learn such representations.
* The paper writing clarity is good and the paper is easy to read. 
* The experiments have been well designed in terms of tasks, robustness studies, ablation studies, and real-robot testing. The authors have also been careful to obtain reliable results with multiple random seed training + testing.

# Major weaknesses

## Incomplete related work comparison
* Section 2: Learning 3D scene representations --- "in contrast to prior work we only use a single fixed view for policy inference, which makes our method both extendable and easy to deploy in the real world." --- prior work such as (Burgess et al., 2019; Lai et al., 2021; Tung et al., 2019a) can also operate with single fixed view during inference (even though their experiments consider the harder case with a moving camera). Why not consider these models / training methodologies as baselines? 

* There is prior work on representation methods that can induce 3D priors into 2D image encoders [R1, R2, R3, R4]. These are closely related to the proposed method and can be directly used as competing baselines (by training on CO3D).

[R1] Hou, J., Xie, S., Graham, B., Dai, A., & Nießner, M. (2021). Pri3d: Can 3d priors help 2d representation learning?. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (pp. 5693-5702).

[R2] Weinzaepfel, Philippe, et al. "CroCo: Self-Supervised Pre-training for 3D Vision Tasks by Cross-View Completion." NeurIPS 2022

[R3] Li, Z., Chen, Z., Li, A., Fang, L., Jiang, Q., Liu, X., Jiang, J., Zhou, B., & Zhao, H. (2022). SimIPU: Simple 2D Image and 3D Point Cloud Unsupervised Pre-training for Spatial-Aware Visual Representations. Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 36(2), 1500-1508. https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v36i2.20040

[R4] Chen, Nenglun, et al. "Self-Supervised Image Representation Learning with Geometric Set Consistency." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022.


## Technical novelty is low

* How is the proposed method different from Lai et al., 2021 (in terms of architectures, loss functions and training methodologies)?
* Key differences I see are the pre-training dataset (CO3D here vs. RealEstate-10k / MP3D in Lai et al.,), vision backbone (ResNet18 here vs. ResNet50 in Lai et al.,) and the use of low-capacity 3D encoder here. 
* If these are the contributions, their importance has not been evaluated in the experiments. A simple way to test this would be to use pre-trained models from Lai et al., trained on RealEstate-10k and MP3D and demonstrate the superiority of pre-training on CO3D with a low-capacity 3D encoder.

## Weak choices of baselines
* Representation learning for RL and robotics is a rich field. The baselines selected do not adequately capture prior work and offer an incomplete picture. Here is a small subset of the entire literature for this problem.
	* Srinivas, Aravind, Michael Laskin, and Pieter Abbeel. "Curl: Contrastive unsupervised representations for reinforcement learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2004.04136 (2020). 
	* Kostrikov, Ilya, Denis Yarats, and Rob Fergus. "Image augmentation is all you need: Regularizing deep reinforcement learning from pixels." arXiv preprint arXiv:2004.13649 (2020).
	* Stooke, Adam, et al. "Decoupling representation learning from reinforcement learning." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021.
	* Yarats, Denis, et al. "Mastering Visual Continuous Control: Improved Data-Augmented Reinforcement Learning." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2021.

* There is also an inconsistency b/w baselines and proposed model in terms of visual backbone and pre-training dataset. The way I see it, there are a few main choices:
	* Pre-training dataset (ImageNet, CO3D, etc)
	* SSL objectives (MoCo-*, MAE, Video AutoEncoder, etc)
	* Vision backbone (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, ViT, etc)
	* Are representations finetuned or not during RL? 
	* Are SSL objectives jointly used to finetune during RL?
* The methods used in the experiments vary wildly in terms of these choices.
	* Proposed method: CO3D + Video AutoEncoder + ResNet-18 + representation finetuning + joint SSL during RL.  
	* MoCo baseline: ImageNet + MoCo + ResNet-18 + representation finetuning + NO joint SSL during RL. 
	* MVP: Human-Object-Interactions + MAE + ViT + NO representation finetuning + NO joint SSL during RL
	* PVR: ImageNet + MoCo + ResNet-50 + NO representation finetuning + NO joint SSL during RL, etc
* Due to these inconsistencies, it is difficult to understand what ultimately benefits the downstream task performance. Statements like "We thus attribute the sizable difference in transfer results between our method and the baselines to the learned 3D representation." may not hold true due to these inconsistencies.
* To show that 3D pre-training matters, the baselines must also use CO3D + <some SSL objective> + ResNet-18 + representation finetuning + joint SSL during RL. **Note:** What would be even better is to find the best combination for each baseline (e.g., CO3D may not be well suited for MVP / PVR --- in which case the best dataset choice can be used). But I can understand that this is too much of an effort and I don't expect the authors to realistically do this.
* Moreover, representation learning methods that induce 3D priors into 2D encoders [R1, R2, R3, R4] are also competing methods for 3D pre-training + finetuning.


## Experiments are only performed on low training regimes
* Why only 500k - 1M steps of experience? 
* This is very low considering sim2real transfer is one of the key experiments. Training for longer in simulation is relatively inexpensive and most methods have not converged. 
* Do trends hold true when all methods are trained for long enough (e.g, 10M / 100M frames)? 


# Minor weaknesses

* Why compare on simple xArm tasks where all methods achieve similar results on 3/4 tasks (see Fig. 5)? 
* "It is not surprising, but recent works (Xiao et al., 2022; Nair et al., 2022; Parisi et al., 2022) only focus on the frozen visual representation, which might neglect the power of end-to-end policy learning" --- why not finetune these representations during RL? Why continue to keep them frozen if that is a limitation of prior work?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper clarity is good. The experimental design is good, but the choices of baselines is poor. Novelty is fairly limited. Hyperparameters and implementation details have been provided for reproducibility, and the authors have promised to release the code.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper has several strengths, but also quite a few weaknesses. The idea is well motivated, the paper writing is clear, and the experiments have been well designed. I appreciate the sim2real transfer as it adds a lot of value to the paper. However, the related work comparison is incomplete, the technical novelty is low, the choices of baselines are poor with quite a few inconsistencies, and the experiment training regimes are very low. These concerns need to be addressed effectively before the paper can be published.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to a combination of 3D reconstruction representation learning with RL training to obtain a policy which may accurately generalize to different sets of RL tasks. The authors illustrate the benefit of this approach on a limited set of a metaworld tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths

**Motivation.** The motivation of the paper makes sense and the introduction reads well -- we live in a 3D world, and it is natural to learn representations that are consistent with underlying 3D world.

# Weaknesses

**Significance.** The paper is only evaluated on a very limited number of underlying tasks -- 4 environments from Metaworld where the underlying performance gain from the approach is rather limited (appears to be nearly identical to from scratch MOCO and imagenet pretraining) which does not give convincing argument on the efficacy of the approach. Furthermore, these evaluated tasks are very simple in nature, and I don't think having 3D structure really helps the approach.  It would be better if the paper were to evaluate on more complex environments in Metaworld, as well as more complex 3D robotic tasks such peg in a whole, or placing a mug on rack, where understanding the 3D geometry of the world is crucial.

**Novel View Synthesis Results.** The reported values on Table 3 are incorrectly labeled -- the SSIM and PSNR columns should be swapped. Furthermore, the PSNR is very poor (13) and indicates near random 3D reconstruction, when methods such as NeRF typically get PSNR values of over 25 and higher. It would be good to see if improving novel view synthesis results would improve the underlying approach.

**Pose Net Predictions.** Pose net suffers significantly when there are rotations between two sets of views -- which occurs commonly in the robotic setting. In the robotic setting, often times the camera poses are known between two images -- can the authors justify the choice of using PoseNet?

**Novelty.** There have been a variety of works integrating NeRF or 3D scene representation learning (https://www.deepmind.com/blog/neural-scene-representation-and-rendering) dating back to 2018, so the novelty of the work is somewhat limited.

**Setup.** What is efficacy of using Co3D as pretraining for 3D representation learning? The environments in Metaworld are synthetic while the images in Co3D are real images. Furthermore, there are backgrounds in Metaworld, so it seems like this type of transfer would be quite out-of-distribution. Can the authors run an ablation on the effect of this representation learning pretraining.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I don't the work is very novel -- the integration of 3D information with reinforcement learning has been explored for a long time, for instance in this paper (https://www.deepmind.com/blog/neural-scene-representation-and-rendering). The paper is generally clear, but there is a major issue with the reported . The underlying results presented in the paper are not very significant and environment evaluated are very toy.
content.summary_of_the_review: I recommend rejecting the paper at this time due to a variety of issues listed above.
